text: A single VNet or VPC can resolve its own private names without much thought. The moment a second network enters the picture, that stops being enough — a workload in one spoke needs to resolve a name that lives in another spoke's zone, or reach an on-premises name during a hybrid migration. This lesson covers how Azure and AWS actually solve that at scale.

Azure's building block is the private DNS zone — created once, holding internal records. But a zone only resolves for VNets it's linked to. A virtual network link connects a zone to a VNet, and that link can cross subscription boundaries, which is what lets one hub-hosted zone serve every spoke without duplicating it per spoke.

Private zones alone don't solve hybrid resolution between Azure and on-premises, though. That's the Azure Private DNS Resolver's job: an inbound endpoint lets on-premises DNS servers query Azure private zones through a private IP, and an outbound endpoint, paired with forwarding rulesets, lets Azure forward specific domains back out to on-premises — one coherent path, in both directions, with no hand-built DNS servers.

AWS's building block is the Private Hosted Zone, Route 53's version of the same idea, associated with VPCs rather than linked — and a zone in one account can be associated with a VPC in another by authorizing that association first. For hybrid resolution, the Route 53 Resolver mirrors Azure exactly: inbound endpoints accept on-premises queries, and outbound endpoints with resolver rules forward specific domains out to on-premises DNS.

That leaves a real organizational choice: let every spoke run its own DNS, which maximizes autonomy but lets every team's configuration quietly diverge, or centralize zones and resolvers in the hub so every spoke links or associates into one consistent, centrally managed setup. Centralized DNS is the pattern that scales, for the same reason centralized egress through the hub scales.

The cost is that a team wanting a genuinely nonstandard DNS configuration has to go through the central team instead of self-serving it — a guardrail worth keeping in mind as the next lesson turns to the broader principles for designing network architecture that holds up as more teams onboard.
